lesson.title: Swapping Partners: Metathesis and the Pull Toward Completion
lesson.summary: Metathesis reactions are double-replacement reactions between ionic compounds in solution, and whether one actually proceeds to a meaningful extent depends entirely on whether it satisfies at least one of the driving forces, precipitate, gas, or water formation, that pull the ion-exchange forward.
lesson.body:
Double replacement describes the general pattern AB plus CD yields AD plus CB, where the positive and negative ions of two compounds trade partners. Metathesis is simply the name chemists use for this same pattern specifically when it happens between ionic compounds dissolved in water, and it is sometimes called an ion exchange reaction. The word metathesis comes from a Greek root meaning transposition, a fitting description of two ions swapping places.

Not every possible ion swap you could write on paper actually happens to any meaningful extent. If you mix two soluble ionic solutions and every possible recombination of ions is also soluble, you simply end up with a beaker containing four kinds of spectator ions floating around together, with no net chemical change worth writing an equation for. A metathesis reaction proceeds in a meaningful, essentially complete way only when it satisfies at least one of the driving forces introduced in the previous chapter: a precipitate forms, which you predict using solubility rules, such as most nitrates being soluble while most halides are soluble except when paired with silver, lead(II), or mercury(I); a gas forms, as when a carbonate reacts with an acid to release carbon dioxide; or a stable, weakly ionized substance like water forms, as in acid-base neutralization.

Here is a worked example of a precipitation metathesis reaction. Lead(II) nitrate reacts with potassium iodide according to Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) to PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq). Lead(II) iodide is insoluble, a bright yellow solid, so the precipitate driving force applies and the reaction proceeds essentially to completion. Suppose 25.0 mL of 0.200 M Pb(NO3)2 is mixed with an excess of KI. What mass of PbI2 precipitate forms?

First find the moles of the limiting reagent, Pb(NO3)2: 0.0250 L times 0.200 mol/L equals 0.00500 mol. The mole ratio between Pb(NO3)2 and PbI2 in the balanced equation is 1 to 1, so 0.00500 mol of PbI2 forms as well. The molar mass of PbI2 is 207.2 g/mol for lead plus 2 times 126.90 g/mol for iodine, which is 253.80 g/mol, giving a total of 461.0 g/mol. The mass of precipitate is then 0.00500 mol times 461.0 g/mol, which equals 2.31 g.

Writing the net ionic equation makes the driving force even clearer: Pb2+(aq) + 2 I-(aq) to PbI2(s), with K+ and NO3- left out entirely because they remain dissolved and unchanged on both sides as spectator ions. Stripping away the spectators like this is exactly how you identify which driving force, if any, is actually operating in a given metathesis reaction.
